subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The causes of war and Just War theory
Holy war, pacifism, terrorism and weapons of mass destruction

questions.q: In the context of religion, peace and conflict, how is 'peace' best defined?
options: The absence of conflict and a state of harmony
The total elimination of all disagreement forever
A treaty signed only by religious leaders
The victory of one side over another in war
questions.explain: Peace is understood as an absence of conflict leading to a state of calm and harmony between people or nations.

questions.q: What is meant by 'justice' in religious teaching about conflict?
options: Bringing about what is right and fair, according to the law
Taking revenge on those who have wronged you
Ignoring wrongdoing to keep the peace
Punishing the innocent alongside the guilty
questions.explain: Justice means bringing about what is right and fair, and ensuring people are treated according to the law and their rights.

questions.q: What does 'reconciliation' mean?
options: Restoring friendly relationships after conflict or disagreement
Refusing ever to speak to an enemy again
Winning an argument by force
Keeping a record of wrongs done to you
questions.explain: Reconciliation is the restoring of friendly relations and bringing people back together after a conflict.

questions.q: In Christian teaching, what does 'forgiveness' involve?
options: Showing grace and mercy, and pardoning someone for what they have done wrong
Forgetting that any wrong ever happened
Demanding an equal act of revenge
Refusing to accept an apology
questions.explain: Forgiveness involves showing grace and mercy by pardoning a wrongdoer and stopping blaming them.

questions.q: Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers'. In which teaching is this found?
options: The Sermon on the Mount
The Ten Commandments
The Lord's Prayer
The Parable of the Sower
questions.explain: 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' comes from Jesus' Sermon on the Mount.

questions.q: Jesus said 'turn the other cheek'. What attitude to conflict does this teaching encourage?
options: A non-violent response rather than retaliation
Immediate armed resistance to any attacker
Ignoring all forms of injustice
Taking an eye for an eye in revenge
questions.explain: Turning the other cheek encourages a non-violent response and refraining from taking revenge on those who wrong you.

questions.q: A man's brother is killed in a robbery, yet he chooses to meet the offender, pardon him and rebuild a relationship. Which two concepts does this BEST illustrate?
options: Forgiveness and reconciliation
Retaliation and greed
Deterrence and proliferation
Pacifism and terrorism
questions.explain: Pardoning the offender is forgiveness, and rebuilding the relationship afterwards is reconciliation.

questions.q: Which theologian is most closely associated with developing Just War theory in the Christian tradition?
options: Thomas Aquinas
Charles Darwin
Martin Luther King Jr
Desmond Tutu
questions.explain: Thomas Aquinas set out key conditions for a just war, building on earlier ideas from Augustine.

questions.q: Which of the following is commonly identified as a cause of war?
options: Greed
Forgiveness
Reconciliation
Pacifism
questions.explain: Greed, self-defence and retaliation are commonly identified causes of war.

questions.q: According to Just War theory, war must only be fought as a...
options: Last resort, when all peaceful options have been tried
First response to any insult
Way of gaining new territory
Means of increasing a nation's wealth
questions.explain: A just war may only be waged as a last resort, after all peaceful means of resolving the conflict have failed.

questions.q: Which of the following is a condition of Just War theory?
options: It must be declared by a legitimate authority such as a government
It must be started by any individual who feels angry
It must aim to destroy as many civilians as possible
It must continue even when there is no chance of success
questions.explain: A just war must be declared and controlled by a proper, legitimate authority such as a government, not by individuals.

questions.q: The Just War condition of 'proportionality' means that...
options: The force and methods used must not be excessive and must match the end sought
As much force as possible should always be used
Only nuclear weapons should be used
Wars should last as long as possible
questions.explain: Proportionality requires that the level of force used is not excessive and is proportionate to the good aimed for.

questions.q: Why might a Christian argue that a war fought purely for greed can never be a 'just war'?
options: It fails the condition of having a just cause and right intention
It uses too few soldiers
It is fought by a legitimate government
It is always fought as a last resort
questions.explain: Just War theory requires a just cause and right intention, so a war fought only for greed cannot be just.

questions.q: A country invades a neighbour to seize its oil fields, attacking without warning and targeting towns. Which Just War conditions are clearly broken?
options: Just cause, last resort and protection of civilians
Reasonable chance of success only
Legitimate authority only
None, because it is fought by a government
questions.explain: Invading for resources lacks a just cause, is not a last resort, and deliberately targeting towns violates the protection of civilians.

questions.q: What is a 'holy war'?
options: A war fought to defend or promote religious belief, believed to have God's support
A war fought only to gain money
A war that uses no weapons at all
A war declared only by non-religious governments
questions.explain: A holy war is fought for a religious cause and is believed to be supported or commanded by God.

questions.q: In Islam, what does 'greater jihad' refer to?
options: The inner, personal struggle to be a good Muslim and follow Allah
A military war against enemies
The building of new mosques
A pilgrimage to Makkah
questions.explain: Greater jihad is the inner spiritual struggle to overcome sin and live according to Allah's will.

questions.q: How does 'lesser jihad' differ from 'greater jihad' in Islam?
options: Lesser jihad is the outward military struggle to defend Islam, under strict conditions
Lesser jihad is the inner spiritual struggle
Lesser jihad means giving to charity
Lesser jihad means daily prayer
questions.explain: Lesser jihad is the outward, physical struggle, including military defence of Islam, which is governed by strict rules.

questions.q: What is 'pacifism'?
options: The belief that violence and war are wrong and disputes should be settled peacefully
The belief that all wars are holy
The belief that weapons should be stockpiled
The belief that revenge is always justified
questions.explain: Pacifism is the belief that war and violence are wrong and that conflicts should be resolved by peaceful means.

questions.q: Which Christian group is well known for its strong tradition of pacifism?
options: The Quakers (Religious Society of Friends)
The Crusaders
The Roman legions
The Zealots
questions.explain: The Quakers are strongly pacifist and reject the use of violence and participation in war.

questions.q: What is 'terrorism'?
options: The unlawful use of violence and intimidation to achieve political or religious aims
A peaceful protest march
A form of international charity
The signing of a peace treaty
questions.explain: Terrorism is the unlawful use of violence and fear, often against civilians, to pursue political or religious aims.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a weapon of mass destruction (WMD)?
options: A nuclear bomb
A standard handgun
A single sword
A wooden shield
questions.explain: Weapons of mass destruction include nuclear, chemical and biological weapons that can kill large numbers of people.

questions.q: What is meant by nuclear 'deterrence'?
options: Possessing nuclear weapons to discourage an enemy from attacking
Using nuclear weapons in every conflict
Getting rid of all nuclear weapons at once
Sharing nuclear weapons with all countries
questions.explain: Deterrence is the idea that owning nuclear weapons discourages enemies from attacking for fear of retaliation.

questions.q: A Quaker refuses to join the army and instead campaigns for peaceful negotiation to end a conflict. Which belief best explains this action?
options: Pacifism
Support for holy war
Belief in nuclear deterrence
Support for terrorism
questions.explain: Refusing to fight and seeking peaceful solutions reflects the pacifist belief that war and violence are wrong.

specSource: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A specification; Theme D: Religion, Peace & Conflict
